title: Capstone Part 2: Modeling, Optimization, and Validation
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Capstone Part 2: Modeling, Optimization, and Validation ##### The 0.91 that was really 0.68 Two students working on the same capstone in Indore submitted models the same week. Both predicted 90-day loan default. Both reported around 0.91 AUC. One of them shipped to a pilot; the other's model was quietly withdrawn after three weeks in production, where it scored 0.68. The difference was not the algorithm — both used LightGBM with almost identical hyperparameters. The difference was the validation protocol. The first student ran `RandomizedSearchCV` over 200 configurations with 5-fold CV, took the best CV score, and reported it as the expected performance. The second ran the same search but *inside* an outer cross-validation loop, and reported the outer score. The first student's 0.91 was the maximum of 200 noisy estimates. When you take the max of 200 draws from a distribution, you get an optimistically biased number — you have selected for configurations that got lucky on those specific folds. The second student's number was 0.87, lower and honest, and it held up in production within half a point. The withdrawn model also had a second problem, invisible until someone looked at SHAP: its top feature was `days_since_last_statement_download`, which was near-zero for defaulters because the collections team downloaded statements when an account went bad. A post-hoc artifact of the collections process, leaking backwards into a "prediction." Part 2 is where your capstone either earns trust or manufactures a number. The technical content is Days 19–22 applied under discipline. The discipline is the deliverable. ##### The modelling ladder Do not start with the most powerful model. Climb deliberately, and record every rung. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Rung 0: Trivial baseline
majority class / global mean"] --> B["Rung 1: Current process
the existing rule, measured"] B --> C["Rung 2: Linear/logistic
regularised, interpretable"] C --> D["Rung 3: Tree ensemble
RandomForest, default params"] D --> E["Rung 4: Gradient boosting
LightGBM/XGBoost, tuned"] E --> F["Rung 5: Blend / stack
only if it clearly earns its keep"] C -.->|"if gap to rung 4 is small"| G["STOP.
Ship the simple model."] ``` Each rung answers a question. Rung 2 tells you whether the signal is essentially linear. Rung 3 tells you whether interactions matter. Rung 4 tells you what careful tuning buys. And the gap between rungs is your evidence for complexity: if logistic regression gets 0.84 and a tuned LightGBM gets 0.855, you have paid a large maintenance and explainability cost for 1.5 points, and the honest recommendation may be to ship the regression. Log every rung to MLflow. The comparison table *is* a deliverable. ##### Cross-validation strategy is a data-type decision The single most common capstone error is `KFold` on data that does not support it. Match the splitter to the structure: | Data structure | Splitter | Why | |---|---|---| | I.I.D. rows, balanced | `KFold(shuffle=True)` | Standard case | | I.I.D., imbalanced target | `StratifiedKFold` | Preserves class ratio per fold | | Repeated entities (customer, patient, device) | `GroupKFold` / `StratifiedGroupKFold` | Stops the same entity in train and test | | Time-ordered | `TimeSeriesSplit` (expanding or rolling) | Never predict the past from the future | | Time + groups | Custom purged/embargoed split | Both constraints at once | | Small n (< ~2,000) | Repeated stratified K-fold | Averages away fold noise | If your data has *both* repeated entities and time ordering — which most real business data does — you need a time-based split with group purging: drop training rows whose entity appears in the validation window near the boundary. Financial ML calls this purging and embargoing, and it matters whenever features have a lookback window that could straddle the split. ##### Nested CV, and when you can skip it Hyperparameter search uses the validation folds to *choose*. If you then report the best validation score, that score is contaminated by the selection. Nested CV separates the two: ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Outer fold 1
train 80% / test 20%"] --> B["Inner CV on the 80%
tune hyperparameters"] B --> C["Refit best config
on full 80%"] C --> D["Score on outer 20%
← unbiased"] D --> E["Repeat for outer folds 2..5"] E --> F["Report mean ± std
of outer scores"] ``` Nested CV is expensive — inner trials × outer folds. Two legitimate shortcuts: - **A held-out test set** you touch exactly once. Simpler and adequate when you have enough data (roughly 10,000+ rows) and the test set is time-forward. - **Nested CV on a subsample** to estimate the optimism gap, then apply that correction to your full-data CV score. What is *not* acceptable is reporting `study.best_value` as your model's performance. State clearly in your write-up which number is the selection score and which is the unbiased estimate. ##### A tracked, tuned workflow end to end ```python import mlflow, optuna, numpy as np from optuna.integration import OptunaSearchCV # or use study.optimize directly from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedGroupKFold, cross_val_score from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, average_precision_score from lightgbm import LGBMClassifier mlflow.set_experiment("capstone-default-risk") optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING) NUM = ["income_monthly", "loan_amount", "tenure_months", "existing_emi_ratio"] CAT = ["employment_type", "state", "product", "channel"] def make_pipeline(params): pre = ColumnTransformer([ ("num", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("sc", StandardScaler())]), NUM), ("cat", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")), ("oh", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", min_frequency=30))]), CAT), ]) return Pipeline([("pre", pre), ("clf", LGBMClassifier(**params, verbose=-1))]) cv = StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42) def objective(trial): params = dict( n_estimators=trial.suggest_int("n_estimators", 200, 1500, step=100), learning_rate=trial.suggest_float("learning_rate", 0.01, 0.25, log=True), num_leaves=trial.suggest_int("num_leaves", 15, 255, log=True), min_child_samples=trial.suggest_int("min_child_samples", 10, 200, log=True), subsample=trial.suggest_float("subsample", 0.6, 1.0), subsample_freq=1, colsample_bytree=trial.suggest_float("colsample_bytree", 0.5, 1.0), reg_lambda=trial.suggest_float("reg_lambda", 1e-3, 30.0, log=True), random_state=42, ) scores = cross_val_score( make_pipeline(params), X_tr, y_tr, groups=g_tr, cv=cv, scoring="average_precision", n_jobs=-1, ) trial.set_user_attr("cv_std", float(scores.std())) return float(scores.mean()) with mlflow.start_run(run_name="lgbm-optuna-v1"): study = optuna.create_study( direction="maximize", sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=42), pruner=optuna.pruners.MedianPruner(n_warmup_steps=5), ) study.optimize(objective, n_trials=120, timeout=3600) mlflow.log_params(study.best_params) mlflow.log_metric("cv_ap_selection", study.best_value) # SELECTION score mlflow.log_metric("cv_ap_std", study.best_trial.user_attrs["cv_std"]) final = make_pipeline(study.best_params).fit(X_tr, y_tr) # Test set touched exactly once, here. p = final.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1] mlflow.log_metric("test_ap", average_precision_score(y_te, p)) # HONEST estimate mlflow.log_metric("test_auc", roc_auc_score(y_te, p)) mlflow.sklearn.log_model(final, "model", input_example=X_te.head(5)) mlflow.log_artifact("reports/optuna_history.html") ``` Three habits embedded here: preprocessing lives **inside** the pipeline so it refits per fold; the selection score and the test score are logged under distinct names so nobody confuses them later; and `input_example` is logged so the model signature is recorded for deployment in Part 3. ##### Comparing models honestly A difference of 0.003 AUC between two models is usually noise. Before you declare a winner: - **Report variance.** Mean ± std across folds. If model A is 0.871 ± 0.014 and model B is 0.868 ± 0.011, they are tied. - **Use paired comparison.** Score both models on the *same* folds and test the per-fold differences. A paired t-test or, better, a corrected resampled t-test accounts for the overlap between CV training sets. - **Bootstrap the test metric.** Resample the test set 1,000 times to get a confidence interval on your headline number. Reporting "test AP 0.412 (95% CI 0.388–0.437)" is the mark of someone who understands their own uncertainty. - **Weigh non-accuracy factors.** Inference latency, model size, training cost, explainability, and how many dependencies you are adding. A 12-model stack that gains 0.004 and takes 40 minutes to retrain is a bad trade. ```python from scipy.stats import ttest_rel import numpy as np scores_a = cross_val_score(model_a, X_tr, y_tr, groups=g_tr, cv=cv, scoring="average_precision") scores_b = cross_val_score(model_b, X_tr, y_tr, groups=g_tr, cv=cv, scoring="average_precision") diff = scores_a - scores_b t, p = ttest_rel(scores_a, scores_b) print(f"A: {scores_a.mean():.4f} ± {scores_a.std():.4f}") print(f"B: {scores_b.mean():.4f} ± {scores_b.std():.4f}") print(f"mean diff {diff.mean():+.4f}, paired p = {p:.3f}") ``` ##### Interpretability and error analysis Once you have a candidate, two things stand between you and deployment. **SHAP** tells you what the model learned. Run it and read the global bar plot with one question in mind: *does the top of this list make sense to a domain expert?* The Indore model's `days_since_last_statement_download` sitting at rank one was a leakage alarm that no validation score could have raised. Then read the beeswarm for direction — if higher income pushes the model towards *more* default risk, either you have found something genuinely interesting or you have a bug, and it is usually a bug. ```python import shap pre = final.named_steps["pre"] clf = final.named_steps["clf"] X_te_t = pre.transform(X_te) names = pre.get_feature_names_out() explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(clf) sv = explainer.shap_values(X_te_t) shap.summary_plot(sv, X_te_t, feature_names=names, plot_type="bar", show=False) shap.summary_plot(sv, X_te_t, feature_names=names, show=False) # Local explanation for the worst false negative — usually the most instructive row. p = clf.predict_proba(X_te_t)[:, 1] worst_fn = np.argmin(np.where(y_te.values == 1, p, np.inf)) shap.force_plot(explainer.expected_value, sv[worst_fn], X_te_t[worst_fn], feature_names=names, matplotlib=True) ``` **Error analysis** tells you where the model fails, which is more actionable than knowing how often. The routine: 1. Rank test errors by loss and read the top 30 by hand. Patterns emerge fast. 2. Slice the metric by every meaningful segment — state, channel, product, ticket size, month, and the fairness groups from Day 42. Build a table sorted by performance ascending. 3. Look for **systematic** failure: a segment where recall is 0.22 against 0.61 overall is a fixable problem (more data, a segment feature, or a separate model). Scattered random errors usually are not. 4. Check calibration by segment with a reliability curve. A model well-calibrated overall can be badly miscalibrated within segments. 5. Write down one failure mode and a concrete plan for it. That is what the assignment asks for, and it is the paragraph interviewers probe hardest. ```python err = X_te.assign(y=y_te.values, p=p) err["decile"] = pd.qcut(err["p"], 10, labels=False, duplicates="drop") by_state = ( err.groupby("state") .apply(lambda d: pd.Series({ "n": len(d), "base_rate": d["y"].mean(), "ap": average_precision_score(d["y"], d["p"]) if d["y"].nunique() > 1 else np.nan, })) .query("n >= 200") .sort_values("ap") ) print(by_state.head(10)) ``` ##### Reproducibility Someone must be able to reproduce your headline number six months from now. That requires: a seed set everywhere (`random_state`, `numpy`, and the framework's own seed), an environment lockfile, a DVC-tracked dataset version, the git SHA logged as an MLflow tag, and the exact split logic in code rather than in a notebook cell. ```python mlflow.set_tags({ "git_sha": subprocess.check_output(["git","rev-parse","HEAD"]).decode().strip(), "data_version": "features_v3", "cv": "StratifiedGroupKFold(5) grouped on customer_id", "notes": "test set untouched until final eval", }) ``` ##### Common mistakes - Reporting `study.best_value` as model performance. - `KFold` on grouped or time-ordered data. - Preprocessing fitted outside the CV loop. - Tuning on the test set by iterating against it "just to check." - Declaring a winner on a difference smaller than the fold standard deviation. - Skipping the linear baseline, so complexity is never justified. - 500 Optuna trials on 3,000 rows — you are fitting the folds, not the problem. - No SHAP review, so leakage survives to production. - Aggregate metrics only, with no slice analysis. - Unlogged runs, so "the good one from Tuesday" is unrecoverable. - Retuning after seeing test results and reporting the new number as unbiased. ##### Hands-on: the tracked ladder Your practical task is the ladder under tracking: baseline, then at least two advanced models with tuned hyperparameters using a CV strategy appropriate to *your* data, then select and interpret the winner with SHAP. Before you run anything, write one sentence in your README naming your splitter and why. That sentence prevents the most expensive mistake available to you. The mini project is the Part 2 artifact: the MLflow comparison log, a rigorously validated final model with reported test performance, SHAP interpretation, and an error-analysis section. Export the MLflow run comparison as a table in your README — a reader should see the ladder and the gaps without launching a UI. Include the confidence interval on your headline metric. The assignment asks you to justify your CV strategy and describe one failure mode with a remediation plan. Be specific: "recall in the ₹10L+ segment is 0.31 against 0.58 overall on 1,140 test rows; the segment is 4% of training data, so I would oversample it and add an interaction between loan size and income band, then re-evaluate that slice specifically." That answer demonstrates you can debug a model, which is a rarer skill than building one. ##### Key takeaways - **Climb the modelling ladder** from trivial to complex, logging every rung — the gaps between rungs are your justification for complexity. - **The CV splitter is a data-type decision**: group by entity, split by time, and combine both when your data demands it. - **Separate selection from estimation.** The tuning score is optimistically biased; report a nested-CV score or a once-touched test set as your honest number. - **Small differences are noise.** Report mean ± std, use paired tests, and bootstrap a confidence interval on your headline metric. - **SHAP and error analysis are validation, not decoration** — they catch leakage that no score can reveal and turn "it's 0.87" into "here is exactly where it fails and what I'd do."
